prompt: A hosting company promises 99% availability. Over a year of 365 days, how much downtime does that allow?
hint: One hundredth of the year.

choices.text: About 52 minutes
choices.why: That is four nines, 99.99%: two more nines than promised.

choices.text: About 8.8 hours
choices.why: That is 99.9%. Each nine divides the allowance by ten, so 99% allows ten times as much.

choices.text: About 87.6 hours
choices.why: Right. 1% of 8760 hours, over three and a half days. It sounds nearly perfect.

choices.text: About 15 minutes a week
choices.why: A week at 99% allows about 1.7 hours, not 15 minutes.

prompt: For a year of 365 days, how many minutes of downtime does 99.99% allow? Give one decimal.
hint: 525,600 minutes in the year, times 0.0001.

prompt: A server fails about once a year. A twin is added that takes over in three seconds. What has changed?
hint: MTBF and MTTR: which one did the twin touch?

choices.text: The server now fails half as often
choices.why: Its MTBF did not move; the server breaks exactly as before.

choices.text: The repair time the customer sees
choices.why: Right. The broken server still waits for a technician; the customer waits three seconds.

choices.text: Nothing, until the broken server is replaced
choices.why: The service is back in seconds, long before anybody replaces anything.

choices.text: Its MTBF and its MTTR both halve
choices.why: The MTBF is untouched, and the repair time as seen from outside fell far more than half.

prompt: An on-call engineer answers every alarm within five minutes and switches to a spare server by hand. Can this service reach five nines over a year?
hint: Five nines is 5.3 minutes a year.

choices.text: Yes, if the spare is already switched on
choices.why: A switched-on spare that waits for a person still waits five minutes.

choices.text: Yes, five minutes is under the allowance
choices.why: Only once, and only if the switch itself takes no time at all.

choices.text: Hardly: one incident spends the whole year
choices.why: Right. 5.3 minutes a year; the response time alone takes nearly all of it, once.

choices.text: It depends on how fast the spare boots
choices.why: The person's five minutes come first, whatever the boot time is.

prompt: A request crosses four parts in series, each available 99.9% of the time. What is the chain's availability, in percent, to one decimal?
hint: 0.999 to the fourth power.

prompt: Two load balancers are each down 0.1% of the time, and their failures are independent. For what share of the time are both down together?
hint: In parallel, multiply the failures.

choices.text: 0.2%, the two shares added
choices.why: Adding is what you would do if either one failing stopped the service: that is series.

choices.text: 0.05%, half of one
choices.why: A second balancer does far better than halving.

choices.text: 0.1%, the same as one
choices.why: That would mean the second balancer adds nothing.

choices.text: 0.0001%, one millionth
choices.why: Right. 0.001 × 0.001. The catch is the word independent.

prompt: In the program's output, two balancers and three web servers still leave 1051.7 minutes of downtime a year. Where is almost all of it?
hint: Which stages are still one machine?

choices.text: In the ISP link and the DNS server
choices.why: Right. They are still single and in series, so they set the ceiling.

choices.text: In the web servers, the weakest at two nines
choices.why: Three in parallel at 99% are down together one millionth of the time.

choices.text: In the balancer pair, which is in series with everything
choices.why: The pair is down one millionth of the time, less than either single part.

choices.text: Spread evenly across the four stages
choices.why: Two of the stages are a million times more reliable than the other two.

prompt: The last design printed 2.1 minutes of downtime a year. Why should that number not be trusted?
hint: What does the parallel formula take for granted?

choices.text: Python rounds percentages badly
choices.why: The arithmetic is right; the assumption behind it is the problem.

choices.text: It assumes twins never fail together
choices.why: Right. Shared power, switches, software and changes make common-mode failures.

choices.text: It leaves out the laptop at the other end
choices.why: The question is about the site; the client's own machine is its own concern.

choices.text: Doubling the ISP halves the traffic each one carries
choices.why: Load does not enter this arithmetic at all.

prompt: Match each shared thing to what separating it looks like.
hint: A pair shares more than a rack.

pairs.right: Two switches, two ISPs in separate ducts
Upgrade one twin, wait, then the other
Change one side and check it before the other

right_distractors: One larger server with more memory

prompt: A fault that takes both machines of a pair down at once, such as one bad configuration pushed to both, is called a ___ failure.
hint: The two share its cause.

prompt: In the lab's data centre, which of these is a single point of failure?
hint: Which one has no twin?

choices.text: lb1
choices.why: lb2 takes over from it; lesson 16 measured the takeover.

choices.text: web2
choices.why: When it stopped, web1 and web3 carried the requests.

choices.text: ns, the DNS server
choices.why: Right. There is one, and without it nobody can find www.example.com by name.

choices.text: The address 192.0.2.80
choices.why: That address moves between lb1 and lb2; either can hold it.

prompt: Which of these are single points of failure in the lab's data centre as drawn? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask of each: if this alone failed, would the request still succeed?

choices.text: The ISP router, isp
choices.why: Right. One router, and every request enters through it.

choices.text: The link from isp into the data centre
choices.why: Right. One link; nothing else enters the room.

choices.text: lb2
choices.why: It has a twin, lb1, which is the point of having two.

choices.text: The DNS server, ns
choices.why: Right. The name lookup happens before the request, and there is one server for it.

choices.text: web3
choices.why: Two other web servers carry its share when it stops.

prompt: Head office has two routers, hq and hq2, but every host's default gateway is 192.168.10.1, which only hq holds. What happens when hq dies?
hint: Where does a host send a packet for the internet?

choices.text: Hosts notice and switch to hq2 by themselves
choices.why: A host has one default gateway and no idea a second router exists.

choices.text: hq2 answers because it is on the same LAN
choices.why: Being on the LAN is not holding the address; nothing moves .1 to hq2 here.

choices.text: The office loses the internet while hq2 sits idle
choices.why: Right. Redundancy the hosts cannot use is not redundancy; lesson 15 fixes it.

choices.text: Traffic slows down but still flows
choices.why: There is no slower path: packets go to a gateway that is not there.

prompt: ns stops, while isp, both balancers and all three web servers are healthy. What does a visitor who has never opened the site see?
hint: What happens before the first packet to 192.0.2.80?

choices.text: The page, served a little more slowly
choices.why: Without an address there is no request to serve slowly.

choices.text: An error that the name cannot be resolved
choices.why: Right. Five healthy machines, unreachable by name. Only cached answers still work.

choices.text: A page from lb2, which takes over the name
choices.why: The balancers share an address, not the job of answering DNS.

choices.text: A 503 error from the balancer
choices.why: The balancer never hears from the browser, which has no address to send to.

prompt: Put the pieces of a failover in the order they happen.
hint: The backup counts silence before it acts.
items: Heartbeats stop arriving at the backup
The backup declares the master dead
The address moves and is announced
Clients update their caches and traffic flows
trap: Declaring the master dead comes after the silence, never at the moment of the failure.

prompt: Why can a backup not take over at the very instant the master dies?
hint: What does a dead machine send?

choices.text: The backup is powered off until needed
choices.why: In VRRP and keepalived the backup is running and listening the whole time.

choices.text: The master sends a goodbye first
choices.why: A machine that dies suddenly sends nothing, goodbye included.

choices.text: Switches block the backup for a few seconds
choices.why: Nothing blocks it; it simply has not concluded anything yet.

choices.text: Silence is its only evidence
choices.why: Right. And silence takes time to be sure of: it waits for several heartbeats to be missing.

prompt: To make failover faster, an engineer sets the backup to take over after one missed heartbeat on a busy link that the pair shares with user traffic. What happens?
hint: A lost packet and a dead machine look the same.

choices.text: The pair flaps whenever the link congests
choices.why: Right. Each congested moment is a takeover, and each takeover costs seconds.

choices.text: Failover becomes instant with no side effects
choices.why: It becomes faster, and it starts firing when nothing has failed.

choices.text: The heartbeats get priority over the user traffic
choices.why: Changing the timeout changes nothing about queueing on the link.

choices.text: The master stops sending heartbeats
choices.why: The master sends as before; some of them are lost on the way.

prompt: HAProxy's checks in lesson 16 run every second and mark a server down after ___ failures in a row, and up again after as many successes.
hint: fall and rise.

prompt: Lesson 15 measured 3.26 seconds of outage when a router's cable was pulled. What is most of that time?
hint: Heartbeats every second, several missed.

choices.text: The time to repair the router
choices.why: Nobody repaired anything; the other router took the address.

choices.text: The backup waiting out the silence
choices.why: Right. Detection is the largest piece; the switch itself is quick.

choices.text: The laptop's operating system rebooting its network
choices.why: The laptop did nothing but keep pinging.

choices.text: The time light takes through the cables
choices.why: The lab has no delay at all; every link is one computer talking to itself.

prompt: What is split brain?
hint: Both machines are alive.

choices.text: Both nodes of a pair crash at the same moment
choices.why: That is a common-mode failure; split brain needs both alive.

choices.text: Both nodes alive, each sure the other is dead
choices.why: Right. The heartbeat link broke, not the machines.

choices.text: A backup that never takes over
choices.why: That is a failover that does not work, which is a different fault.

choices.text: Traffic divided evenly between two nodes
choices.why: That is active-active balancing, and it is deliberate.

prompt: A cluster has 5 voters. How many of them can fail while the rest still hold a majority?
hint: A majority of 5 is 3.

prompt: A team adds a fourth node to a three-node cluster to make it safer. How many more failures can the cluster now survive?
hint: A majority of 4 is 3.

choices.text: One more: four survive two
choices.why: Two failures leave two of four, which is not a majority.

choices.text: Two more, since each node doubles safety
choices.why: Nodes do not multiply safety; a majority has to survive.

choices.text: None: four survive one, just as three do
choices.why: Right. It adds a machine that can break and no failure survived.

choices.text: It depends on which node is the leader
choices.why: Quorum counts voters, whoever leads.

prompt: What does fencing do before a survivor takes over?
hint: STONITH.

choices.text: Asks the other node politely to stop
choices.why: A node that cannot be heard cannot be asked either.

choices.text: Adds a firewall rule in front of the cluster
choices.why: Fencing acts on the other node, not on the clients.

choices.text: Copies the other node's data to the survivor
choices.why: That is replication; fencing is about who may write.

choices.text: Makes sure the other node is off
choices.why: Right. By cutting its power or its storage: certain rather than hopeful that one side writes.

prompt: Two database servers share one rack and one switch. They replicate to each other, fail over automatically after one missed heartbeat, and have no witness. Which risk is the most serious?
hint: Data, one lost heartbeat, two voters.

choices.text: A slightly slower failover than with three nodes
choices.why: Speed is the least of it; this pair takes over too eagerly, not too slowly.

choices.text: Split brain, with both sides accepting writes
choices.why: Right. One lost packet, no quorum, no fencing, and two diverging copies.

choices.text: The rack's power, which the switch also shares
choices.why: A real common-mode risk, and it stops the service; split brain corrupts the data.

choices.text: Replication using too much of the switch
choices.why: Congestion matters here only as the thing that loses a heartbeat.

prompt: A site is one ISP link at 99.9% in series with a web pair whose combined availability is 99.9999%. What is the site's availability in percent, to two decimals?
hint: The weakest serial part sets the ceiling.
